doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Required chapel and Dean Alfange
summary: Chapel rules, atheist students' alternative meetings, and a reunion encounter with classmate Dean Alfange.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Oh. Did you have chapel every day?
I think you had chapel on Sunday, yes.
And I think you had three chapels a week. I’m not sure, you’d have to check.
And this is something you were supposed to go to? You were required to go?

Oh you had to. You were allowed three cuts. It was like anything else. I think you were allowed three cuts a semester, in a course, and chapel was the same. You got three cuts. By the time I was a junior some of us had said, “Well look, we’re atheists, what’s this Sunday chapel?” So they allowed us to have a meeting, a philosophic meeting with one of the professors, I’ve forgotten who, to take the place of that. But we had to do something, you know, we couldn’t opt out.
Yeah. Well on top of all those things that you were, you were also a jazz guy.
Well that’s probably more to the point here. You got me wandering around.
No but I enjoy hearing about — of course I should tell — my daughter went to Hamilton, she just graduated last May so I really enjoy hearing about what it was like back then.

Yeah, well Hamilton was a conservative college, and it still is. And did you know Dean Alfange, a member of my class? I hadn’t seen Dean since I graduated. I went back for my fiftieth, and Dean came over and said “Jim, I don’t know whether you remember me.” And I said “sure Dean, nice to see you.” And we sat and talked and drank a glass of wine and he had said something nice about one of my books. And I asked, because his father had been head of the — I’m not sure, one of the labor parties, whether it was the American Labor Party or something, but he had been very much on the left, a Labor guy, like me. And I said “Dean, how did you end up here at Hamilton.” And he said “my dad
went here.” So that was somebody I think had sponsored him, an immigrant or something like this sponsored him and he came. I mean you’d have to ask Dean the details.
